newsitem.title: USA: NBC finds daytime a hard market to crack.
newsitem.headline: NBC finds daytime a hard market to crack.

text.p: Even taking television viewers to a bright, sunny beach in the middle of winter is not helping NBC make a dent in the important daytime TV market.

When NBC was developing the first new soap opera to debut on daytime television in eight years, and looking for a setting to appeal to viewers' taste for fantasy, the answer was at first too obvious to see.

The beach, after all, does not seem so special when you can see it from your home or on your morning commute, or at the very least have easy access to it on weekends -- the way most southern California based-television writers do. But then the network polled viewers around the country and conceived of the new soap opera "Sunset Beach" as a way to boost daytime ratings.

"An extraordinary number of people we polled said they would like to see it set on the beach," said Robert Guza, head writer of "Sunset Beach," which began airing in January. "It fulfils a kind of fantasy thing. Precious few people live on a beach."

Even fewer live on a beach that resembles the set of "Sunset Beach." While the drama purportedly takes place in southern California, it actually combines spectacular California sunsets with a New England quaintness and locals who are so friendly and so up on their neighbours' business that they seem to have come out of a small town in the Midwest.

As such, "Sunset Beach" is a bit of a change for producer Aaron Spelling, whose past creations like "Beverly Hills 90210" and "Melrose Place," set in trendy west Hollywood, feature Los Angeles prominently. The show's melodrama and fast-moving plots, on the other hand, are vintage Spelling.

But even with the help of market research, a producer whose name is synonymous with popular television, and a promotional campaign larger than any other in NBC's history, "Sunset Beach" has had a hard time making a dent in the daytime market.
In its first eight weeks on the air, it consistently came in 10th in market share out of the 11 daytime dramas ranked in the Nielson Television Index, ahead of only ABC's "The City."

NBC, which already holds the No. 1 market position in prime time and late night television, says it hopes "Sunset Beach" will be the vehicle through which it can dominate the daytime market as well. But it is finding resistance unusually strong.

Unlike primetime television, where new sitcoms and dramas are always appearing and a good new show can quickly win viewers, the daytime market is ruled by fierce loyalties to longstanding shows. Most popular daytime dramas like CBS' "The Young and the Restless" and NBC's "Days of our Lives" were created decades ago and have pools of viewers who have watched for that long and even gotten their children or grandchildren hooked.
In addition, at a time when fewer people overall are watching any daytime television, soap operas need viewers to tune in day after day rather than just once a week.

"Gaining a soap opera viewing audience is so unlike prime time, where all viewers have to do is watch once a week, NBC spokeswoman Dianne Passarelli said. "We're asking for at least a two to three day-a-week commitment. And we realise that because of that we literally have to get (viewers) hooked."

Along with the dreamy locale that "Sunset Beach" exploits with extensive on-location shooting in the Orange County town of Seal Beach, NBC is trying to appeal to younger viewers with trendier fashions than what is typically seen on daytime television and contemporary issues such as Internet romance.
After the show's unremarkable debut, NBC says it is going back to strengthen story lines and add more romance.

It insists it will keep it on the air for two years before it even considers cancelling it. But it also admits to having some question about whether soap operas are still the best way to get viewers to turn on the television in the middle of the day.
"NBC is very committed," Guza said. "The question is whether the climate is right."
